title: Unit 5b - Copy and Assignment Title Slide
summary: Title slide for Unit 5b on Copy and Assignment in CS103, taught by Mark Redekopp. Covers copy constructors, assignment operators, and deep vs shallow copy.
main_text: This unit covers Copy and Assignment in C++, including the this pointer, copy constructors, assignment operator overloading, shallow vs deep copy, and the Rule of Three. These concepts are essential for managing objects that contain dynamically allocated memory.
notes_text: This unit is part of the Objects 2 section of CS103 and builds on operator overloading from Unit 5a. Understanding copy semantics is critical for writing correct C++ classes, especially those that manage heap memory.

title: Side Topic: The this Pointer - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the 'this' pointer topic. Asks how an object refers to itself from inside a member function.
main_text: This section covers a side topic: How does an object refer to itself from inside a member function? The answer involves the 'this' pointer, which is an implicit pointer passed to every member function that points to the calling object. Understanding the this pointer is a prerequisite for the copy constructor and assignment operator topics that follow.
notes_text: The this pointer is essential background for understanding copy constructors and assignment operators, particularly why the assignment operator returns *this and why copy constructor parameters must be passed by reference.

title: The this Pointer - How Member Functions Know Their Object
summary: Explains that 'this' is an implicit pointer passed to member functions so they know which object's data to operate on. Shown via a Deck class example.
main_text: How do member functions know which object's data to be operating on (d1 or d2)? The object (d1) is implicitly passed via a special pointer called the 'this' pointer. When you write d1.shuffle(), the compiler translates this to Deck::shuffle(Deck *this) with 'this' pointing to d1's address (0x720). Inside the actual code you write, you access members directly: cards[i], cut(). The compiler-generated code uses this-> explicitly: this->cards[r], this->cards[i], this->cut(). The memory diagram shows two Deck objects: d2 at 0x7e0 and d1 at 0x720, each with cards[52] and top_index members. The 'this' pointer holds 0x720, pointing to d1.
notes_text: The this pointer is always implicitly available inside member functions. You rarely need to write 'this->' explicitly (the compiler adds it for you), but there are important cases where you must use it: when parameter names shadow member names, and when returning *this from assignment operators.

images.description: Memory diagram showing two Deck objects (d1 at 0x720 and d2 at 0x7e0) with cards arrays and top_index, and the 'this' pointer holding 0x720 pointing to d1. Side-by-side comparison of actual written code vs compiler-generated code with this->.

title: The Same Names Problem - Parameter Shadowing
summary: Shows the bug when constructor parameters have the same names as data members. The compiler uses the closest definition, so name=name assigns the parameter to itself.
main_text: If arguments and data members have the same name, the compiler chooses the 'closest' defined variable. This can lead to problems! Example: class Student { public: Student(string name, int id, double gpa); ~Student(); private: string name; int id; double gpa; };. In the constructor Student::Student(string name, int id, double gpa), the assignments name = name; id = id; gpa = gpa; are all self-assignments of the parameters to themselves. The data members remain uninitialized (shown as ???, ??, ??). The constructor arguments hold the correct values ('Tina', 123, 3.8), but the circular arrows show that each assignment just writes the parameter back to itself.
notes_text: This is a common bug. When a parameter has the same name as a data member, the parameter 'shadows' the member. The compiler sees 'name = name' and assigns the parameter to itself, never touching the data member. The fix is shown on the next slide using the this pointer.

images.description: Diagram showing Object Data Members (this->) with uninitialized values (???) on the left, and Constructor Arguments with correct values on the right, with circular arrows showing self-assignment

title: Using this to Resolve Name Shadowing
summary: Shows the fix: use this-> to explicitly refer to data members when parameters have the same names. this->name = name correctly assigns the parameter to the member.
main_text: If arguments and data members have the same name, the compiler chooses the 'closest' defined variable. This can lead to problems! The fix: use this-> to explicitly refer to the data members. Student::Student(string name, int id, double gpa) { this->name = name; this->id = id; this->gpa = gpa; }. Now the assignments work correctly: this->name refers to the data member, and plain 'name' refers to the parameter. The diagram shows arrows flowing from the Constructor Arguments (Tina, 123, 3.8) correctly into the Object Data Members, which now hold the proper values.
notes_text: While using this-> works, the better practice in C++ is to use different naming conventions (e.g., name_ for members or m_name) to avoid shadowing entirely. However, understanding this-> is essential for the assignment operator which must return *this.

images.description: Diagram showing correct data flow from Constructor Arguments to Object Data Members using this-> prefix, with red arrows indicating successful assignment

title: What We Currently Know About Copying Objects - Section Divider
summary: Section divider introducing the topic of what students currently understand about object copying before learning copy constructors and assignment operators.
main_text: This section reviews what students currently know about copying objects, including the default member-by-member copy behavior of C++ structs and classes, before introducing the need for custom copy constructors and assignment operators.
notes_text: This sets up the problem that copy constructors and assignment operators solve: the default shallow copy behavior is insufficient for objects with dynamically allocated memory.

title: Object Assignment - Member-by-Member Copy
summary: Assigning one object to another performs a member-by-member copy of all data members. C++ does this automatically for structs and classes.
main_text: Assigning one object to another will perform a member-by-member copy of the entire source object to the destination object. Example with a student struct: struct student { char name[80]; int id; int major; };. In main: student s1, s2; strncpy(s1.name, "Jill", 80); s1.id = 5; s1.major = CECS; s2 = s1;. The assignment s2 = s1 copies all members: name, id, and major are each copied from s1 to s2. The memory diagram shows s1 at address 7300 and s2 at address 7388, with yellow arrows indicating the member-by-member copy. Normally, C/C++ performs only one operation at a time, but object assignment is an exception -- it copies all members in one statement.
notes_text: This default behavior works perfectly for simple types (ints, arrays of chars, etc.) that don't involve pointers to heap memory. The problem arises when objects contain pointer members that reference dynamically allocated data, as will be shown later.

images.description: Memory diagram showing s1 and s2 structs in memory with yellow arrows indicating member-by-member copy of name, id, and major fields between addresses 7300 and 7388

title: Copy Semantics - Section Divider
summary: Section divider for the main topic of copy semantics, covering copy constructors and assignment operators in detail.
main_text: This section covers Copy Semantics, specifically copy constructors and assignment operators. These are the mechanisms C++ provides for controlling how objects are duplicated, and understanding them is critical for writing correct classes that manage resources.
notes_text: Copy semantics is one of the most important topics in C++ OOP. Misunderstanding shallow vs deep copy leads to some of the most common and dangerous bugs: double-free errors, use-after-free, and memory leaks.

title: Copy Constructors - Introduction and Motivation
summary: Introduces the need for a copy constructor: a constructor that builds a new object as a copy of an existing object, e.g., Complex c3(c1).
main_text: Write a prototype for the constructor that would want to be called by the highlighted line of code: Complex c3(c1);. This creates a new Complex object c3 by making a copy of c1. The class has: Complex(); (default constructor) and Complex(double r, double i); (parameterized constructor). The question asks: what constructor definition do I need for c3's declaration? We want a constructor that will build a new Complex object (c3) by making a copy of another (c1). Realm of Reasonable Answers are explored on the next slide.
notes_text: The copy constructor is distinct from the assignment operator. The copy constructor creates a NEW object initialized as a copy, while the assignment operator copies data into an EXISTING object. Complex c3(c1) creates c3 and initializes it as a copy of c1 in one step.

title: Copy Constructor Prototypes - Three Options
summary: Evaluates three copy constructor prototypes: Complex(Complex) won't work (infinite recursion), Complex(Complex&) is possible, Complex(const Complex&) is best.
main_text: Write a prototype for the constructor that would want to be called by Complex c3(c1);. Realm of Reasonable Answers: Complex(Complex); -- We will see that this can't be right (it causes infinite recursion because passing by value requires a copy, which calls the copy constructor, which requires a copy...). Complex(Complex &) -- Possible, but not ideal. Complex(const Complex &) -- Best! Making a copy shouldn't change the input argument, thus 'const'. We want a constructor that will build a new Complex object (c3) by making a copy of another (c1). The const reference is the correct signature.
notes_text: The const reference parameter is essential for two reasons: (1) const because copying should not modify the source object, and (2) reference because pass-by-value would trigger another copy constructor call, creating infinite recursion. This is why Complex(Complex) is fundamentally broken.

title: Assignment Operators - operator= for Already-Existing Objects
summary: The assignment operator (operator=) is called when an already-in-scope object is reassigned. Its signature returns a reference and takes a const reference.
main_text: The assignment operator (operator=(...)) is called when an object that is ALREADY in scope is reassigned. Its signature is: Complex& operator=(const Complex& other);. Why does it return by reference? We will see soon (it enables chaining like c4 = c3 = c2). Do we need to define this function in our class? The compiler provides a default version. Example: Complex c1(2,3), c2(4,5); Complex c3(c1); // Copy constructor. c3 = c2; // Assignment operator -- translates to c3.operator=(c2);. The key distinction: copy constructor creates a new object, assignment operator copies into an existing one.
notes_text: The distinction between copy construction and assignment is subtle but critical. Copy construction: object is being created for the first time (Complex c3(c1) or Complex c3 = c1). Assignment: object already exists and is being overwritten (c3 = c2 after c3 was already constructed).

title: Default Assignment and Copy Constructors
summary: C++ compiler auto-generates default copy constructor and assignment operator, both performing element-by-element (shallow) copy of data members.
main_text: C++ compiler automatically generates a default copy constructor: called when an object is allocated and initialized to be a copy of another object of the same type. Signature: Complex(const Complex&);. Called by either Complex c3(c1); or Complex c3 = c1;. Simply performs an element-by-element copy. C++ compiler automatically generates a default assignment function: called when you assign to an object that is already allocated (memory already exists). Simply performs an element-by-element copy. Signature: Complex& operator=(const Complex&);. Example: Complex c3(c1); // copy constructor. Complex c4(5,7); c4 = c2; // default assignment operator, c4.operator=(c2). The diagram shows c4 and c2 as Class Complex objects with real_ and imag_ members, with an arrow showing the element copy.
notes_text: Both defaults do the same thing: element-by-element copy of data members. This works perfectly for classes with only simple data types (int, double, char arrays). The problem arises with pointer members, which is the motivation for custom implementations.

images.description: Diagram showing two Complex objects c4 and c2 with real_ and imag_ data members, with an arrow indicating element-by-element copy from c2 to c4

title: What Gets Called - Copy Constructor vs Assignment with =
summary: Clarifies that Complex c4 = c1 calls the copy constructor, not the assignment operator, even though it uses = syntax, because c4 is being created.
main_text: What gets called when we use '=' when creating a new object? It may look like an assignment operator. But C++ will call the Copy Constructor!! Example: Complex c3(c1); // copy constructor -- obvious. Complex c4 = c1; // This ALSO calls the copy constructor, not operator=. The key distinction: c4 doesn't exist yet, it is being created and initialized in one step. Since c4 is a new object being declared, C++ uses the copy constructor. The assignment operator would only be called if c4 already existed: Complex c4; c4 = c1; // THIS calls operator=.
notes_text: This is a common source of confusion. The = sign in 'Complex c4 = c1;' is NOT the assignment operator -- it is copy initialization syntax, which invokes the copy constructor. The rule: if the object is being declared for the first time on the left of =, it is copy construction. If it already exists, it is assignment.

title: MyArray Class - Default Copy/Assignment Problem Setup
summary: Introduces a MyArray class with a pointer member to illustrate the problem with default copy/assignment. Shows how a1 is constructed with dynamic allocation.
main_text: The compiler automatically generates default copy constructor and assignment function. The MyArray class has: int *dat; int len;. The normal constructor: MyArray::MyArray(int d[], int num) { dat = new int[num]; len = num; for(int i=0; i < len; i++) { dat[i] = d[i]; } }. In main: int vals[] = {9,3,7,5}; MyArray a1(vals,4); MyArray a2(a1); // calls default copy. MyArray a3 = a1; // calls default copy. MyArray a4; a4 = a1; // calls default assignment. The diagram shows a1 after construction: a1.dat = 0x200, a1.len = 4. After new, dat points to uninitialized memory at 0x200. After the constructor loop, the array at 0x200 contains [9,3,7,5].
notes_text: This is the critical setup slide. The MyArray class owns dynamically allocated memory (new int[num]). The question is: how are the contents of a2, a3, a4 related to a1? The default shallow copy will only copy the pointer value, not the data it points to.

images.description: Memory diagram showing vals array [9,3,7,5], a1 with dat=0x200 and len=4, and the dynamically allocated array at 0x200 containing [9,3,7,5] after construction

title: Shallow Copy Problem - All Objects Share Same Data
summary: Shows the disaster of default shallow copy: a1, a2, a3, and a4 all have dat pointing to the same address 0x200. Modifying one affects all others.
main_text: Default copy constructor and assignment operator make a SHALLOW COPY (data members only) rather than a DEEP copy (data members + what they point at). The diagram shows: A1: a1.len = 4, a1.dat = 0x200. A2: a2.len = 4, a2.dat = 0x200. A3: a3.len = 4, a3.dat = 0x200. A4: a4.len = 4, a4.dat = 0x200. All four objects point to the same dynamically allocated array at 0x200 containing [9,3,7,5]. This means: modifying through any object changes the data for all of them, and when the destructor is called for each object, the same memory at 0x200 will be deleted multiple times (double-free error).
notes_text: This is the central problem that motivates custom copy constructors and assignment operators. Shallow copy copies only the pointer value (0x200), not the data it points to. All four objects now share the same underlying array, leading to aliasing bugs and double-free crashes.

images.description: Memory diagram showing four MyArray objects (A1-A4) all with dat=0x200 and len=4, with arrows all pointing to the same array at 0x200 containing [9,3,7,5]

title: When to Write Copy Constructor - Shallow vs Deep Copy
summary: Rules for when to write custom copy constructors: needed when you have pointer members pointing to dynamically allocated data that should be independently copied.
main_text: Default copy constructor and assignment operator ONLY perform SHALLOW copies. SHALLOW COPY: data members only. DEEP copy: data members + what they point at. Analogy: like saving a webpage to your HD -- a shallow copy saves the page but doesn't copy the pages linked to. You SHOULD/MUST define your own copy constructor and assignment operator when a DEEP copy is needed: When you have pointer data members that point to data that should be copied when a new object is made. Often times, if your data members are pointing to dynamically allocated data, you need a DEEP copy. Corollary: If a Shallow copy is acceptable, then you do NOT need to define a copy constructor.
notes_text: The guideline is straightforward: if your class uses new/delete (dynamic allocation), you almost certainly need custom copy constructor, assignment operator, and destructor. If your class only has simple types or objects that handle their own copying (like std::string, std::vector), the defaults are fine.

title: Defining Copy Constructors - Implementation
summary: Shows how to implement a copy constructor for MyArray. It takes a const reference, allocates new memory, and copies the actual data for a deep copy.
main_text: Same name as normal constructor but should take in an argument of the object type. Usually a const reference: MyArray(const MyArray&);. Class declaration includes: MyArray(const MyArray& rhs);. Implementation: MyArray::MyArray(const MyArray &rhs) { len = rhs.len; dat = new int[len]; // copy from rhs.dat to dat }. The key steps: (1) copy the length, (2) allocate NEW memory with new int[len], (3) copy the actual data from rhs.dat to the newly allocated dat. This creates an independent copy -- modifying one object's data won't affect the other. Usage: MyArray a2(a1); // deep copy. MyArray a3 = a1; // also deep copy.
notes_text: The critical step is 'dat = new int[len]' -- this allocates fresh memory for the new object's data, rather than copying the pointer from rhs. Then the data is copied element-by-element into this new memory. This is what makes it a deep copy.

title: Implicit Calls to Copy Constructor - Pass-by-Value
summary: The copy constructor is implicitly called when passing objects by value to functions. The function's parameter is constructed as a copy of the argument.
main_text: Recall pass-by-value passes a copy of an object. If defined, the copy constructor will automatically be called to make this copy; otherwise the default copy will perform a shallow copy. Example: class Complex { public: Complex(); Complex(double r, double i); Complex Complex(const Complex &rhs); ~Complex(); double real, imag; };. Copy constructor: Complex::Complex(const Complex &c) { cout << "In copy constructor" << endl; real = c.real; imag = c.imag; }. Function: int dummy(Complex rhs) { cout << "In dummy" << endl; }. In main: Complex c1(2,3); int x = dummy(c1); // Copy Constructor implicitly called on c1 to create rhs.
notes_text: This is an important implicit use of the copy constructor. When you pass an object by value to a function, the copy constructor is called to create the parameter. This is why pass-by-reference (or const reference) is preferred for large objects -- it avoids the copy constructor call entirely.

title: Why Copy Constructor Must Take Reference - Chicken/Egg Problem
summary: Explains why Complex(Complex) causes infinite recursion: passing by value requires a copy, which calls the copy constructor, which requires a copy, forever.
main_text: Write a prototype for the constructor that would want to be called by Complex c3(c1);. Now we see why the first option can't be right: Complex(Complex c); -- BAD! Because to pass c1 by value requires a copy to be made, which calls the copy constructor, which requires another copy... it's a chicken/egg problem (infinite recursion). Complex(const Complex &c); -- GOOD! The argument must be passed by reference to avoid the infinite recursion. Using a reference means no copy needs to be made to pass the argument, breaking the cycle.
notes_text: This is a fundamental design constraint of copy constructors. If the copy constructor took its argument by value, calling it would require making a copy, which would call the copy constructor, which would need to make a copy... ad infinitum. Passing by reference avoids creating any copy of the argument.

title: Defining Copy Assignment Operator - Initial Implementation
summary: Shows implementing operator= for MyArray. Called when an already-existing object is assigned to. Allocates new memory and copies data for deep copy.
main_text: operator=() is called when an object already exists and then you assign to it. Copy constructor is called when you assign during a declaration (e.g. MyArray y=x;). Assignment operator is called when you assign to an object that has ALREADY been constructed. Example: MyArray z; // constructed. z=x; // now assigned. Can define operator '=' to indicate how to make a copy via assignment. Implementation: MyArray& MyArray::operator=(const MyArray &rhs) { len = rhs.len; dat = new int[len]; // copy from rhs.dat to dat }. Gotchas? Yes -- this version has problems that will be addressed on the next slide.
notes_text: This initial implementation has two critical bugs: (1) it doesn't free the old dat memory before allocating new memory (memory leak), and (2) it doesn't check for self-assignment (a1 = a1 would delete data then try to copy from deleted memory). These gotchas are addressed next.

title: Assignment Operator Gotchas - Memory Leak and Self-Assignment
summary: Two gotchas: (1) must delete old data before allocating new to prevent memory leaks, (2) must check for self-assignment (this == &rhs) to avoid data loss.
main_text: Gotchas? Destination object may already be initialized and simply overwriting data members may lead to a memory leak. Self assignment (which may also lead to memory leak or lost data). The corrected implementation: MyArray& MyArray::operator=(const MyArray &rhs) { if(this == &rhs) return *this; // self-assignment check. if(dat) delete dat; // free old memory. len = rhs.len; dat = new int[len]; // allocate new memory. // copy from rhs.dat to dat. return *this; }. In main: MyArray a1(vals1,4); MyArray a2(vals2,4); a1 = a1; // self-assignment -- handled by check. a2 = a1; // normal assignment.
notes_text: The self-assignment check (if(this == &rhs)) is essential. Without it, a1 = a1 would delete a1's data, then try to copy from the now-deleted data. The delete before new prevents memory leaks from the old allocation. The return *this enables chaining.

title: Assignment Operator Practicals - Return Type and Chaining
summary: RHS should be const reference (no copy, no modification). Return should be a reference (*this) to enable chained assignments like c4 = c3 = c2.
main_text: RHS should be a const reference: Const so we don't change it. Reference so we don't pass-by-value and make a copy (which would actually call a copy constructor). Return value should be a reference: Allows for chained assignments. Should return (*this). Reference so another copy isn't made. Example: Complex& Complex::operator=(const Complex & rhs) { real = rhs.real; imag = rhs.imag; return *this; }. Usage: Complex c3, c4; c4 = c3 = c2; // same as c4.operator=(c3.operator=(c2));. The chaining works because c3.operator=(c2) returns a reference to c3, which is then passed to c4.operator=().
notes_text: The return type Complex& (reference) is critical. If it returned Complex (by value), chaining would still work but would create unnecessary copies. Returning *this by reference is efficient and correct. The const reference parameter avoids both modification and copying.

title: Assignment Operator Overloading - Multiple Type Support
summary: Shows overloading operator= for different RHS types. Complex can accept both Complex& and int& as assignment sources, with chaining working across types.
main_text: If a different type argument can be accepted we can overload the = operator. The Complex class declares: Complex &operator=(const Complex &r); and Complex &operator=(const int &r);. The int version: Complex& Complex::operator=(const int& r) { real = r; imag = 0; return *this; }. Usage: Complex c1(3,5); Complex c2, c3, c4; c2 = c3 = c4 = 5;. This chains as: c2 = (c3 = (c4 = 5)); First c4.operator=(5) calls the int& version, sets real=5, imag=0, returns *this. Then c3.operator=(c4) calls the Complex& version. Then c2.operator=(c3) calls the Complex& version.
notes_text: The chaining example c2 = c3 = c4 = 5 demonstrates how different overloads of operator= can work together. The rightmost assignment uses the int& version, while subsequent assignments use the Complex& version. The return type Complex& is consistent across all overloads.

title: Copy Constructor Summary and the Rule of Three
summary: Key summary: Rule of Three states if you need any one of copy constructor, assignment operator, or destructor, you need all three. Usually triggered by dynamic memory.
main_text: If you are okay with a shallow copy, you don't need to define a copy constructor or assignment operator. Rule of Three: If you need more than the default of any of the following: a copy constructor, an assignment operator, and a destructor, then you need all 3 (i.e. if you need 1 you need all 3). Usually this applies if you have dynamically allocated memory. Copy constructor should accept a const reference of the same object type. Assignment operators should be careful to cleanup initialized members and check for self-assignment. Assignment operators should return a reference type and return *this.
notes_text: The Rule of Three is one of the most important C++ design rules. The reasoning: if you need a custom destructor (to free dynamically allocated memory), then you also need a custom copy constructor and assignment operator (to properly deep copy that memory). Omitting any one leads to bugs.

title: Exercises For Home - IntList Practice
summary: Practice exercises: implement -=, ==, copy constructor, and assignment operator for a singly-linked IntList class.
main_text: Suppose you are given a class that implements a singly-linked list of integers (with a head pointer data member). Exercises: Write a '-=' operator that takes one element and removes it from the list if it exists. Write a '==' operator that checks whether the contents and order of one list matches another. Write a copy constructor and assignment operator. The test code shows: IntList m1, m2; m1.push_back(5); m2.push_back(5); if(m1 == m2) { cout << "Should print!"; }. m2.push_back(7); m2 -= 5; // now m2 would just have [7]. IntList m3(m1); // make a copy of m1. m3.push_back(8); // m3 should have [5,8]. m2 = m1; // assignment.
notes_text: These exercises combine operator overloading from Unit 5a with copy semantics from 5b. A linked list with a head pointer is a prime example of where deep copy is needed -- shallow copy would share the same linked nodes, leading to double-free when destructors run.

title: Review Section Divider
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of review questions for copy constructors and assignment operators.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the Review section with practice questions on copy constructors, assignment operators, the Rule of Three, and shallow vs deep copy.
notes_text: Students should attempt these review questions to verify their understanding before looking at the solutions.

title: Review 1 - Copy Constructor Prototype Question
summary: Review question: what is the correct prototype for the copy constructor? Options are Complex(Complex), Complex(Complex&), and Complex(const Complex&).
main_text: What is the correct prototype for the copy constructor call when c3 is created in the code: Complex c3(c1);? Options: Complex(Complex); -- bad (causes infinite recursion, will be shown to be incorrect). Complex(Complex &) -- possible but not ideal. Complex(const Complex &) -- correct answer (const because copying shouldn't modify the source, reference to avoid infinite recursion).
notes_text: This review tests the fundamental understanding of why the copy constructor must take a const reference. The infinite recursion argument is the key: pass-by-value triggers a copy, which calls the copy constructor, which triggers another copy...

title: Review 2 - Copy Constructor vs Assignment Operator Identification
summary: Review: identify which function is called in each scenario. Also asks what kind of copy the default versions perform (shallow).
main_text: Which function? For each of the following, identify whether the copy constructor is called or the assignment operator: Complex c1; Complex c2 = c1; -- which one? Complex c1; Complex c2(c1); -- which one? Complex c1, c2; c2 = c1; -- which one? Default Versions: What kind of copy does the default copy constructor and assignment operator perform? The MyArray class has: int* data; // ptr to dynamic array. size_t len;. Students must determine whether shallow or deep copy is the default.
notes_text: Answers: (1) copy constructor (c2 is being created), (2) copy constructor (explicit copy construction syntax), (3) assignment operator (c2 already exists). Default performs shallow copies -- only the pointer value is copied, not the data it points to.

title: Review 3 - Rule of Three and Assignment Operator Questions
summary: Review questions: state the Rule of Three, identify extra considerations for operator= vs copy constructor, and determine the return type of operator=.
main_text: State the Rule of 3. Assignment Operator: What extra considerations does the assignment operator need to handle vs. the copy constructor? What should operator= return? The MyArray class has int* data (pointer to dynamic array). A skeleton for MyArray& operator=(const MyArray& other) is shown for students to complete.
notes_text: Expected answers: Rule of Three -- if you need any one of destructor, copy constructor, or assignment operator, you need all three. Extra considerations for operator=: self-assignment check and cleaning up old data. Return type: *this (which is of type Obj&).

title: Solutions Section Divider
summary: Section divider marking the beginning of solutions to the review questions.
main_text: This slide marks the beginning of the solutions section for the review questions on copy constructors, assignment operators, and the Rule of Three.
notes_text: Students should attempt the review questions before looking at these solutions.

title: Review 1 Solution - Copy Constructor Prototype Answer
summary: Solution: Complex(const Complex&) is best. Complex(Complex) causes infinite recursion. Complex(Complex&) is possible but doesn't protect against modification.
main_text: What is the correct prototype for the copy constructor call when c3 is created? Complex(Complex); -- We will see that this can't be right (causes infinite recursion through pass-by-value copying). Complex(Complex &) -- Possible (avoids infinite recursion by using reference). Complex(const Complex &) -- Best! Making a copy shouldn't change the input argument, thus 'const'. The const qualifier provides compile-time protection against accidentally modifying the source object during the copy.
notes_text: The progression from Complex(Complex) to Complex(const Complex&) teaches important lessons about C++ parameter passing: pass-by-value is dangerous for copy constructors, and const correctness should always be applied when the function doesn't intend to modify the parameter.

title: Review 2 Solution - Copy Constructor vs Assignment and Shallow Copies
summary: Solutions: Complex c2 = c1 and Complex c2(c1) both call copy constructor. c2 = c1 (after c2 exists) calls assignment. Defaults perform shallow copies.
main_text: Which function? Complex c1; Complex c2 = c1; -- copy constructor (c2 is being created and initialized). Complex c1; Complex c2(c1); -- copy constructor (explicit copy construction syntax). Complex c1, c2; c2 = c1; -- assignment operator (c2 already exists, being reassigned). Default Versions: What kind of copy does the default copy constructor and assignment operator perform? Shallow Copies! Only the data members are copied, not what pointers point to. For a class with int* data and size_t len, the default copies the pointer value and len, but both objects end up sharing the same dynamically allocated array.
notes_text: The first two cases are both copy construction even though they look different syntactically. The = in 'Complex c2 = c1' is copy initialization, NOT assignment. The critical rule: if the object on the left is being declared for the first time, it is copy construction regardless of = syntax.

title: Review 3 Solution - Rule of Three and Assignment Operator Answers
summary: Solutions: Rule of Three means needing any one of destructor/copy ctor/operator= means you need all three. operator= must handle self-assignment, cleanup, and return *this.
main_text: State the Rule of 3: If a class needs to define ANY ONE of the destructor, copy constructor, or assignment operator, THEN it very likely needs to define ALL 3! Having pointers to dynamically allocated data would generally necessitate deep copies and a destructor to deallocate! Assignment Operator: What extra considerations does the assignment operator need to handle vs. the copy constructor? Self assignment and cleaning up old data. The copy constructor doesn't need these because the object is brand new (no old data to clean up, and self-assignment is impossible during construction). What should operator= return? *this (which is of type Obj&) -- enables chaining and avoids unnecessary copies.
notes_text: The Rule of Three is a cornerstone of C++ resource management. The reasoning is airtight: if you need a destructor to free dynamically allocated memory, then shallow copies would leave dangling pointers after the original is destroyed. Therefore you need deep copies via custom copy constructor and assignment operator.
